newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Nordic airlines team up against local giant SAS.
newsitem.headline: Nordic airlines team up against local giant SAS.

text.p: Three Nordic airlines said on Wednesday they planned to step up cooperation, in a move seen as closing ranks against Scandinavian airline SAS .

Finnish flag-carrier Finnair, privately-owned Norwegian airline Braathens SAFE and domestic Swedish airline Transwede Airways said they would unveil closer cooperation plans at a news conference on April 3.
Analysts said this news, which teamed Braathens SAFE up with traditional SAS rival Finnair for the first time, was a logical step in an equation which spells tougher times ahead for SAS.
"If you want to fight a giant, you need a lot of money...so it makes sense that you do it with other airlines," said aviation analyst Lars-Gunnar Comen.

The three airlines had already been chipping away at market share on what local analysts call the golden triangle, the profitable routes between the Scandinavian capitals of Stockholm, Copenhagen and Oslo.

Norwegian group Braathens SAFE last November launched regular flights between Oslo and Stockholm and has said it plans a further offensive in the region including a frequent flyer programme which is linked to British Airways.

Danish airline Maersk Air said it would launch regular flights between Copenhagen and Stockholm next month which will share codes and have joint airport handling with Finnair while offering cheaper fares than SAS.
Braathens SAFE owns half of Transwede and holds an option to buy the remaining 50 percent.

"The next step would be Copenhagen-Oslo, the last place where SAS still has a monopoly," said one Oslo-based industry analyst. "But this would be tough because most travellers to Copenhagen are headed further, down to Europe."
Analysts stopped short of saying the move was part of a larger offensive by British Airways, which last week said it had strong expansion plans for the Nordic region.
"But I wouldn't be surprised," one analyst said. "British Airways is very aggressive."

Instead analysts said the cooperation would probably be limited to code sharing, or possibly a frequent flyer programme. SAS has kept Scandinavian passengers loyal through a strong frequent flyers incentive programme.
SAS, which is partly owned by the governments of Sweden, Denmark and Norway, shrugged off the announcement.
"This deal is one of the scenarios we outlined would emerge for the home market," SAS spokesman Peter Forssman told Reuters.
"We have had these airlines as competition one-by-one earlier. Now that they are closing up their relationships we are not astonished," he said.
"Competition, which was the whole idea of the deregulation of the industry, is now here. We will do our best to fulfil our part," he added.
But beating SAS on its home turf will not be easy.
"SAS certainly has problems -- increasing competition and high costs -- but it's still a major carrier and they have a lot of money in their deep pockets," Comen added.
